name: 07-drivers-esp32
description: What carries the frame out of a device: the LED pins only real hardware has, the panel protocols, and the network senders it shares with a desktop.

steps.title: Drivers on a device
steps.caption: Drivers on a device. Real pins, real panels.
A driver carries the finished frame out of the device. The list is the same one a computer offers, but on this chip the pin drivers have real pins to clock.
This is the one most rigs start with. R M T is a peripheral on the chip that was built for infrared remotes, and it turns out to clock addressable LEDs exactly as well.
Pin eighteen, where the strip is wired on this device. That one field is the whole answer to how a frame reaches a light.
Start and count are the slice of the buffer this driver takes. A count of one is the smallest job there is: the single light built onto the device.
Back to everything, and now the card objects. One pin clocks about two thousand lights before the refresh becomes a slideshow, and this wall is four thousand of them.
There it is in the status line, in the driver's own words: some lights are not driven, add pins or use start and count.
So give it a second pin. Eighteen and thirty eight, the two LED pins this device brings out, and the warning clears: two thousand lights each, and the buffer split between them.
One driver, two strands, and the bit timing in nanoseconds if your strip needs it. Most never do: the defaults are the W S twenty eight twelve numbers.
Out again. A driver is a module like any other, so it comes and goes on the next frame and the lights never stop.
This is the one that makes a wall possible. Sixteen strands clocking out at the same time, one pin each, all fed from the same buffer.
Same two pins, but clocked side by side rather than one after the other. On a device wired for it that list is sixteen pins long.
Sixteen lanes in parallel is how twelve thousand lights refresh without tearing. It is the same effect output, cut into strands and sent out at once.
And away. Nothing else in the tree changes when a driver leaves.
H U B seventy five is a different animal. These are the panels you see on a stage backdrop, and this drives them straight from the chip's own pins with no receiving card in between.
Bit depth is the trade it asks you to make: more bits is a smoother gradient, fewer bits is a faster refresh.
Out it goes.
And this one talks to the receiving cards a professional rig is built from, over raw Ethernet frames below I P, the way a sender card does.
Removing it, so what is left is the set a computer has too.
The network senders work here exactly as they do on a computer. Art Net, s A C N and D D P, out to fixtures that listen on the network rather than on a pin.
Those, and the video senders and the Hue bridge, all behave the same on a device as on a desktop, so the drivers clip on the computer shows them in full.
One frame, and any of these carries it. What a device adds is not more drivers, it is hardware for the ones that need it.
